name: Mobile App Backend
tagline: The server side of a phone app: delta sync, presigned uploads, push and a version gate
summary: A backend for an iOS and Android client, built around the three facts that make mobile different from the web: the network is unreliable, the app on the device may be two years old, and you cannot hotfix it. Everything here exists to make those survivable — delta sync so a screen renders offline, a remote config carrying a minimum supported version, and push as a pointer rather than a payload.

nodes.label: Mobile App
nodes.why: Renders from a local database first, then reconciles with the server, so a weak signal never produces an empty screen.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: Images dominate mobile bytes; serving them from an edge cache cuts latency on cellular and keeps egress off the origin.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.role: TLS, token check, rate limit, routing
nodes.why: One entry point so authentication, throttling and version headers are enforced once rather than in every service.

nodes.label: Config & Flags
nodes.role: Remote config, feature flags, minimum supported version
nodes.why: The only way to change a shipped app's behaviour without a store release — which is also the only recovery path for a bad build.

nodes.label: Auth Service
nodes.why: Login runs in the system browser and returns a short-lived access token with a refresh token in the platform keystore, so a stolen device backup is not a stolen session.

nodes.label: Product API
nodes.role: Reads and writes for product features
nodes.why: Screen-shaped endpoints rather than fragments: one request per screen keeps the radio asleep and the battery alive.

nodes.label: Sync Endpoint
nodes.role: Changes since a cursor, and queued writes in
nodes.why: A delta rather than a full refresh: the client sends its cursor and receives only what changed, which is what makes sync affordable on a metered connection.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: Feed and catalogue reads are repeated across every client; the counters behind per-device throttling need to be shared and fast.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Every row carries an updated-at and a soft-delete marker, because a client asking 'what changed?' needs to learn about deletions too.

nodes.label: Object Storage
nodes.why: The app uploads directly with a presigned URL, so a 20MB video never passes through the API and a failed upload can resume.

nodes.label: Message Queue
nodes.role: Decouples the request from the fan-out
nodes.why: A push gateway outage should become a backlog, not a failed user request or a lost notification.

nodes.label: Push Worker
nodes.why: Keeps the device-token table alive: it consumes unregistered-token feedback and deletes dead tokens instead of sending to them forever.

nodes.label: APNs / FCM
nodes.why: Delivery is best effort and unacknowledged, which is why the payload carries an id and the app fetches the real state.

nodes.label: Crash & Analytics
nodes.why: Client-side request timing segmented by app version and connection type is the only place p95 on cellular is visible.

flows.name: Cold start on a bad network
steps: The app renders immediately from its local SQLite copy — no spinner, no network needed.
It calls the gateway, which enforces TLS, the rate limit and the app-version header.
Remote config returns feature flags and the minimum supported version; too old, and the app shows an upgrade wall.
The access token has expired, so the refresh token is exchanged for a new one in the background.
The sync endpoint is called with the client's cursor: 'what changed since this point?'
PostgreSQL returns changed and deleted rows; the app merges them and the screen updates in place.

flows.name: Upload a photo
steps: The app records the pending upload durably, then hands it to the OS background transfer session.
It asks the API for a presigned URL through the gateway — a small, fast request.
The API returns a URL scoped to one object key with a short expiry; nothing large touches the API.
The device uploads straight to object storage and the OS resumes it after the app is suspended.
The CDN serves the stored object to every other client from an edge near them.

flows.name: Notify a user who is not in the app
steps: A product action produces an event; the request returns without waiting for any notification.
The queue holds it, so a gateway outage becomes a backlog rather than a lost notification.
The worker looks up this user's live device tokens, applies preferences and quiet hours, and deduplicates on the event id.
APNs or FCM accepts the payload — accepted, not delivered; unregistered tokens come back as feedback and are deleted.
The device shows the alert; tapping it deep-links into the app, which fetches the real state because the payload was only a pointer.

decisions.decision: Sync a delta against a cursor, not a full refresh
decisions.why: A client on cellular cannot afford to re-download a dataset it already has, and a full refresh makes the first screen slow exactly when the network is worst. A cursor turns sync into a small, resumable request.
decisions.tradeoff: Every table now needs an updated-at and a soft-delete marker, and the client needs merge logic. Deletions are the part teams forget, and the symptom is rows that never disappear.

decisions.decision: Upload media directly to object storage with a presigned URL
decisions.why: Large uploads through the API tie up request capacity, cannot resume, and fail entirely when the app is suspended mid-transfer. A presigned URL lets the OS background transfer own it.
decisions.tradeoff: The API no longer sees the bytes, so validation, virus scanning and thumbnailing move to a storage event handler — and the URL's scope and expiry become a security boundary you must get right.

decisions.decision: Remote config carries a minimum supported version
decisions.why: You cannot recall a shipped build. A server-controlled version gate plus feature flags is the only mechanism that can turn off a broken feature or require an upgrade, and it has to exist in the first release to be useful later.
decisions.tradeoff: An upgrade wall is a hostile experience and locks out users who cannot update, so the bar for using it must be high — and every flag is a code path that stays in the binary.

decisions.decision: Push carries an identifier, not the state
decisions.why: Push is best effort, unordered and size-limited, and the payload renders on a locked screen after passing through a third party. Sending an id means a dropped notification costs one round trip instead of correctness.
decisions.tradeoff: Every notification tap costs a request, and the app must handle the case where the referenced entity has since changed or been deleted.

versions.title: One API
versions.summary: The app calls a REST API which reads the database. Fine until the first user opens it on a train and sees an empty screen.

versions.title: Offline and media
versions.summary: A sync endpoint with cursors makes the app usable offline, media moves to object storage behind a CDN, and a cache absorbs repeated reads.

versions.title: Push, config and visibility
versions.summary: Notifications go through a queue and a worker that owns the token table, remote config adds a version gate and flags, and client crashes and timings are collected per app version.

textAlternative: A mobile app on the left talks to an API gateway, which fronts four services: remote config and feature flags (including a minimum supported version), an auth service for sign-in and token refresh, a product API, and a sync endpoint that returns changes since a client-supplied cursor. The product API reads through a Redis cache to a PostgreSQL system of record; the sync endpoint reads changed and deleted rows from the same database. Media is uploaded by the device directly to object storage using a presigned URL obtained from the API, and served back through a CDN. Product actions publish events to a message queue, which a push worker consumes: it looks up device tokens, applies user preferences, and sends to APNs or FCM, which delivers a pointer-shaped notification to the device. The app also reports crashes and client-side request timings to an analytics and crash ingest service.
